questions.question: What does the 'testing effect' claim about retrieval practice?

answerOptions.text: Trying to recall information is itself a powerful way to learn it, often beating re-studying
answerOptions.rationale: Retrieval is a learning event, not just measurement — producing an answer from memory strengthens it.

answerOptions.text: Tests are only useful for grading, not for learning
answerOptions.rationale: This is the misconception the testing effect overturns; low-stakes testing is a study technique.

answerOptions.text: You should only test yourself right before an exam
answerOptions.rationale: Retrieval works best distributed over time, not crammed at the end.

answerOptions.text: Recognizing the answer is as effective as recalling it
answerOptions.rationale: Recognition is weaker than producing the answer from memory; the effort is what helps.

questions.hint: Think about why a quiz can teach, not just measure.

questions.question: Which schedule best reflects spaced practice with expanding intervals?

answerOptions.text: Same day, then ~2 days, then ~1 week, then ~2–4 weeks
answerOptions.rationale: Each successful recall lets you push the next interval further out.

answerOptions.text: Five reviews back-to-back in one evening
answerOptions.rationale: That's massed practice (cramming) — it feels productive but decays fast.

answerOptions.text: One review, only on the night before the test
answerOptions.rationale: A single late review can't flatten the forgetting curve over time.

answerOptions.text: Review every hour, forever, at a fixed interval
answerOptions.rationale: Intervals should expand as recall succeeds, not stay fixed and tiny.

questions.hint: The gaps should grow as you succeed.

questions.question: Why does interleaving (ABCABC) often beat blocked practice (AAABBBCCC) for retention?

answerOptions.text: It forces you to repeatedly choose which approach applies, building the real skill
answerOptions.rationale: Discriminating between problem types is the skill you need later; blocking lets you autopilot.

answerOptions.text: It lets you avoid the harder topics
answerOptions.rationale: Interleaving doesn't skip difficulty; it adds desirable difficulty.

answerOptions.text: It always produces better immediate performance
answerOptions.rationale: Blocked practice usually gives better *immediate* performance; interleaving wins on retention/transfer.

answerOptions.text: It removes the need for spacing
answerOptions.rationale: Interleaving and spacing are complementary, not substitutes.

questions.hint: What do you have to decide every time the topic switches?

questions.question: What is elaborative interrogation?

answerOptions.text: Asking 'why' a fact is true and how it connects to what you already know
answerOptions.rationale: Building explanatory links creates more retrieval routes to the memory.

answerOptions.text: Re-copying your notes in neater handwriting
answerOptions.rationale: That's an encoding activity with little retrieval or elaboration.

answerOptions.text: Highlighting every important sentence
answerOptions.rationale: Highlighting is passive encoding and rated low-utility by the research.

answerOptions.text: Memorizing definitions word-for-word
answerOptions.rationale: Rote memorization lacks the explanatory connections elaboration builds.

questions.hint: It starts with a one-word question.

questions.question: Why does re-reading feel effective but often isn't?

answerOptions.text: It builds familiarity (fluency illusion), which we mistake for real knowledge
answerOptions.rationale: Recognizing text isn't the same as being able to produce the idea on demand.

answerOptions.text: It is a form of retrieval practice
answerOptions.rationale: Re-reading is encoding, not retrieval — nothing is recalled from memory.

answerOptions.text: It creates desirable difficulty
answerOptions.rationale: Re-reading is easy and smooth — the opposite of desirable difficulty.

answerOptions.text: It spaces your practice automatically
answerOptions.rationale: Re-reading in one sitting is massed, not spaced.

questions.hint: Smooth and familiar is not the same as known.
